item.title: Ralliston's Journey through all of the 001 proposals - Part Four - spikebrennan's proposal
item.content:encoded:
Review: Goddamnit, I love this one to bits. Whilst I will say that I think it is just a bit too short, the table at the beginning serves almost no purpose1, I cannot not love it. It's really, really creative, at the same time being really in character for the Foundation. Them making a deal with God is pretty much what I'd expect from the O5 Council.

All that being said however, it is kinda… too little? I feel like it should be just a bit longer. Not saying it should be super long, absolutely not; but just something more to chew on would be nice in my opinion.

Result: +1

Footnotes
1. As yes, we already know no one can die here, and just showing us this is kinda… not needed, really?

item.content:encoded:
While I too loved the phrase "tactical theology," it's going to have to be a downvote for me. Not because I'm extremely devout and the claim that God could have a blind spot offends me (I am and it does, but I'm perfectly willing to let such cases of artistic license slide if they manage to produce a good story), but because this article feels like two separate concepts that've been crudely attached together with bubblegum and paperclips.

I mean you've got a location into which God's Omniscience and Omnipresence do not extend -a concept which, in any narrative that runs on Abrahamic Theology and Metaphysics, would literally be as much of an Eldritch Abomination That Should Not Be as it could possibly get- but all that changes when you cross it's boundaries is that people can't die anymore. Except when they die from certain causes. That's like if you wrote an SCP comprising a drink made from the literal bile of Yog-Sothoth itself, but all that happens to you when you drink it is you get a little gas. Unless you drink it with certain meals.

+ show block
– hide block

Also, the idea of finding an area of ground into which God cannot see and proceeding to make it the site of a new Covenant with God makes about as much sense as finding a building made entirely out of living meat and converting it into a church for the broken god.

The concept of a building in which people cannot die would be perfectly valid as an SCP (albeit probably not 001-proposal material). The idea of SCP-001 being God Almighty themself is an excellent idea (albeit one redundant with Dr Clef's proposal).

…but trying to frankenstein them together into the same SCP feels like you just decided to combine two different SCPs together and consulted one of those "First letter of First name and First letter of Last name" tables.

Also, I think that fieldstone had a point in what he said earlier: that the Foundation would be more likely to respond to meeting God by "[slapping] and SCP designation on him and amnesticizing Christians faster than you can say 'Gnosticism.'" So if you want to write an 001 proposal that ends with the O5s taking a Covenant with God, but wanted to respect both Christian canon and (what passes for) Foundation canon, then I'd recommend a sequence of events somewhere between TheGreatHippo's proposal, Kalinin's proposal, and the 12 plagues of Egypt: one where God progressively makes things worse for the Foundation and is in complete control the whole time, but all the while the O5s refuse to admit that what they are up against is God Almighty, to admit that they have finally come up against a foe more powerful than themselves and which they cannot hope to beat, or to admit defeat.

Also, since 001 proposals are technically supposed to represent the source (or, in some cases, the end) of all anomalies, and Literal Divine Intervention is certainly one possibility, I'd suggest explaining some of the more troublesome SCPs for the Foundation (such as 682 or Samothras) as themselves being some of the 12 Plagues of the Foundation.


As a courtesy to our readers on mobile devices, please collapse long posts. ~Zyn

item.content:encoded:
Necropost response here from the author:

There is no canon, as we all know - but that doctrine describes the absence of a general universal canon covering the entire body of SCP literature.

Individual SCP articles can be, and should be, and are, understood as each having their own siloed, stand-alone canon. In other words, generally speaking each SCP article is in its own universe. (By author fiat, my 001 proposal shares a canon with a few other examples of my body of work, such as SCP-1844, SCP-2336, SCP-4336 and SCP-4436.) But moving on…

One of the themes of my body of SCP writing is starting from a real-world theological or folklore premise (in the sense that the idea already exists in the real world, not that I'm expecting my reader to accept the theology or folklore as fact), accepting it completely at face value as if it is objective fact in the stand-alone canon of the writing piece, imagining the Foundation confronting it, and seeing where that leads.

Here, my jumping point is essentially: "In this canon, you can have either biblical inerrancy or an omnipotent God. But not both, because there seem to be some scriptural passages that are incompatible with an omnipotent God. So in this canon, biblical inerrancy is the one that we actually have."

And everything else here follows from that.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
"The Office of Tactical Theology" is now among my top-ten favorite phrases on the entire site. I bet they've produce mathematical models on how Akiva radiation interacts with Pascal's Wager.

The prose and voice throughout this piece are excellent; there's a splendid sort of humor running throughout it that manages to remain understated despite being so utterly absurd. The article never quite breaks character and winks at the reader, but you very much get the sense it would like to. I think that element — being funny while coming off as trying very hard to be serious — is among my favorite aesthetics among SCP articles.

I feel like this could have worked quite well as something other than an 001 proposal, however. That's a mild complaint; I can understand why it's an 001 (the anomaly is in a position of incredible importance within the context of its own narrative), but I feel like it could have succeeded much more spectacularly had it not had to work against the expectations readers carry when they encounter an 001.

Nevertheless, this was a lot of fun and filled with wonderful, sinister little twists of fridge logic. It was an easy upvote from start to finish.

item.content:encoded:
EDIT: Just noticed that someone addressed this earlier in the comments. Although I disagree with THAT person's particular interpretation of the passage as well, it's true that there's no real consensus among scholars. What I write below is just what seems most reasonable to me.

ORIGINAL: While this is awesome, and I upvoted, I would like to comment on the fact that the Newton passage is actually a mistranslation from the Bible, taken somewhat out of context, and conflates the end of one verse with another. In the verse before, God has commanded Moses to go before the Pharaoh and demand that he let the Israelites go; but Pharaoh, having had his heart hardened by God, will refuse, and thusly have his son killed. Having foreknowledge therefore of Pharoah's refusal, God seeks after Pharoah's son in an inn—the proper translation is "sought to kill him", not "tried to kill him". That part with "tried to met him - meaning Moses" is both not found in the original Hebrew and a misattribution of the term "him" to Moses, when the proper text makes it fairly clear that it's Pharoah's son.

The next bit, with the circumcision, is actually the next verse, and refers to an entirely separate incident in which Moses and his wife circumcise their son. The "he let him go" part refers to Moses letting his son go after restraining him during the procedure. Zipporah, who is not exactly a Jew, is disgusted with the procedure, which is where the "bloody husband" (more properly translated as "bridegroom of blood") comes from. While seemingly a non-sequitur, this is not thematically separate from the previous verse, as the only thing distinguishing Hebrews from Egyptians is their circumcised status. Moses is likely rushing to do this procedure to save his son's life from the wrath of God.

(Source: interest in theological history, some skill in Hebrew, experience with multiple translations of the Bible)

That all being said though, this is truly an awesome 001, and I'm a big fan. I'm just a nitpicker.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Did you mean you intentionally misread (you said you "read" in your comment) the source text? If so that's fine for anyone who isn't familiar with the source text, and perfectly valid as a writing technique, honestly. I don't take issue with that as a technique. I simply have to comment that as someone familiar with this passage I can't get over how wrong the interpretation is.

Newton's interpretation (along with the interpretation that serves as the bedrock for this article) was objectively incorrect because even the King James Version includes Exodus 4:26 where it states: "So he (God) let him (Moses) go." The underlying cause of the threat was solved when Moses's wife circumcised their son.

God didn't try and fail to kill Moses. God began to kill Moses and then stopped once God's demands was satisfied.

Now that's all assuming we pretend the KJV is the one version of the bible and is the actual word of god. If we take even a slightly deeper look at the original sources we find the whole thing doesn't stand up at all.

Both the Septuagint and going back further to the Chaldee or Aramaic sources will change the meaning of this whole thing. Instead of god trying to do the killing it's the "Angel of the Lord". Instead of it being a case of trying to kill him it's "sought to kill him". Instead of it being an inn it's a "resting place".

We can examine "sought" as it's a much more nuanced word than "try" which is the problem with that translation. From "sought" we can infer that God (or the Angel he sent to do this) at that moment wanted to kill Moses and began the process of doing so. This doesn't have to be a lightning bolt or Moses falling over dead. God can choose any method he wants to kill Moses. The fact that it was a non-instantaneous method of killing is backed up by "So God let Moses go" following the successful circumcision.

Essentially, in order for the interpretation to hold up, we have to assume god is only capable of killing Moses instantly, and failed to do so. If any method of killing is available to God other than an instantaneous kill, the whole conceit falls apart.

So I intentionally misread the source text. You caught me. (It's not like this phenomenon is unknown to literature- Dan Brown basically bases his whole career on this technique, and he's not even a good writer.) Hell, some scholars argue that passages and concepts in the New Testament are basically the outcome of doing this to the Old Testament.

I'm a little puzzled by your assertions that this is an "objectively incorrect interpretation." While I accept that the interpretation that I'm putting in Isaac Newton's mouth is certainly not the best interpretation, the scholarship that I've seen doesn't seem to come to any kind of consensus about this passage other than the fact that it's opaque, and that the pronouns in the original are confusing and potentially ambiguous. My personal opinion is that there was a bad edit at some point in history and clarifying information somehow got left on the cutting room floor.

The English language version that I put in there is direct from the KJV. And I'm sure you're aware of what happens when whack-a-doodle religious movements decide to apply the concept of scriptural inerrancy to a difficult passage.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Superb prose. Appeals precisely to my sense of humour. However, I have to downvote.

It breaks, and then craps all over, my suspension of disbelief. In other scips that deal with faiths – Abrahamic or otherwise – there is some measure of ambiguity; there is room to imagine that the belief systems, rituals or myths described in that article somehow represent a bastardised, second-order version of a more mechanistic truth, or an accidental happening-upon a workable fudge.

But there's no seeing through a glass darkly here: the gist of this article is that the Christian God is real, every chapter of the Christian Bible is 100% true, and the actual God of the literal Old Testament smites you with actual lightning when you piss him off. Also, devils are real, and you become immortal if you outsmart God. And all death happens because of wibbly-wobbly radiationy-waviationy stuff.

I'm fundamentally opposed to this idea because the entire conceit of the site is explaining supernatural phenomena as if they were natural science. It seems thematically unfit to invoke one more supernatural phenomenon to explain all the others. Particularly because – and I think this underpins everything I've said above – you don't borrow nearly enough of the phraseology of science, and that which exists here feels handwavy and perfunctory.

I can imagine liking this if the execution weren't so blunt and humour-focused. I need more plausibility in my scips, especially if you're going to pull the religion card.

Let me end on a positive note. "Tactical Theology", "killed in a meteorological event", "Faraday cage for sin", First Commandment in the contract: these remind me of the very best of Douglas Adams. Your ability to match disparate writing styles, as shown in the archival documents, is among the best I've seen on this whole site. It's just that the concept doesn't match my idea of how the site should be. It's too silly.

Stone tablets are expected, but I have asked for a .pdf file as well.

I wanted to upvote so bad here. I love the concept, but a few things stop me. Mainly, this just ramps up too quickly. This is an 001 proposal, so I feel like there's room for more table setting before you get to the big reveal, namely, the Foundation has entered into a covenant with God himself. That's a HUGE concept, but we go from "god's blindspot" to "Office of Tactical Theology" (which I love) pretty quickly, without any real explanation for the details on how this whole process goes. As it is, I'm left with the implication that God just spoke into the mind of an 05 (or Katz?) one day, out of the blue and said "let's make a deal!".

I think there's room for some meat there. Without it, I feel like we jumped from just past the starting line, right to finish. The anomaly is solid, and I like where this proposal ends up. I just feel like I need more in-between.

Also, re: Akiva radation, I also had no idea what it was, and I would recommend at least inserting a short footnote at its first mention to clarify it. I don't think it would be immersion breaking, as even in-universe, very few (namely, one, from the link provided) SCPs reference this unit.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
There's a lot of wasted potential here, but the thing that likely ruined it for me was the Biblical bits. Exodus 4:24-25 being quoted out of context is annoying. The language of the verses does not lend itself to the interpretation here. Essentially the whole article is predicated on an objectively incorrect interpretation of Exodus.

There's a lot of context behind this event, that god was angry with Moses because he put off the circumcision of his son at his wife's request and yadda yadda yadda but the important bit to remember is Exodus 4:26 which is what happens after the quoted bits.

"So he (God) let him (Moses) go: then she (Moses's Wife Zipporah) said, A bloody husband thou art, because of the circumcision."

This lets you know that whatever god was doing to kill Moses wasn't an instantaneous thing (most biblical scholars believe Moses was stricken with disease here). This is the real problem with imperfect translations. The word "tried" should've likely been "began" like this: "And it came to pass by the way in the inn, that the Lord met him, and began to kill him."

Also, and this is neither here nor there but it wasn't an inn. The original text indicated only that it was an overnight resting place.

I would like to like this. But knowing what I know about the premise I can't really get into it. I'd say that means it rests on the execution but the execution here is only ok, and not great.

Apologies, but it's a -1 from me.

If people don't die in the area with no Akivas, that means that God's grace is killing *everyone, all the time*. That has some huge philosophical implications that you could have turned to, and really made this something weighty. As it is, this is disappointing.

item.title: Re: Reluctant -1
item.content:encoded:
Well, akivas are mentioned in a part of SCP-1844 that's covered by a collapsible so perhaps you missed it.

Anyway, once more with feeling. The akiva is the SI derived unit of divine grace, comparable to the lumen being the SI derived unit for measuring the total quantity of visible light emitted by a source. It's not explicitly explained in the article for the same reason that an article about a sound-based SCP subject would not, for example, explain what is meant by "decibel."

Generally speaking there's a background level of akivas everywhere in the universe (except, as it turns out, within the Inn), sort of the same way we have the cosmic microwave background (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_microwave_background). There are also specific things that are akiva sources, such as certain relics, holy places and people.

The thaumometer is an instrument that measures akivas.
